title: Percept histories are not physical states
stem: An agent has three possible percepts and two possible actions. It acts after each history of length one or two. Count unrestricted deterministic agent functions and memoryless percept policies. Explain the difference.
solution: There are $3$ histories of length one and $3^2=9$ of length two, so a full table has $12$ independent entries. Each entry selects one of two actions, giving $2^{12}=4096$ tables. A memoryless policy assigns one action to each of three current percepts, giving $2^3=8$ policies. The full table can choose different actions after histories $(x,z)$ and $(y,z)$, while the memoryless policy must use the same action for both because their final percept is $z$. This is a syntactic count over all histories; a fixed environment may make some histories unreachable, so distinct tables can behave identically there.

title: The empty-history convention
stem: There are two percepts, three actions and a horizon of two percepts. How does permitting an action before any percept change the agent-function count?
solution: Without an initial action, table entries correspond to $2+4=6$ nonempty histories, so there are $3^6=729$ functions. If an action is also assigned to the empty history, one additional entry appears. It can independently choose one of three actions, giving $3^7=2187$. The factor is three, not a factor of two or an extra history at every depth. This convention does not change the environment's physical state count; it changes the domain on which the behavioural function is specified.

title: One percept does not eliminate time dependence
stem: An agent always observes the same percept and chooses from four actions over five decisions. Count arbitrary history-based functions on these decision histories and stationary memoryless policies.
solution: There is exactly one history of each length, so the five decision histories are distinct by length even though every symbol is identical. Each can receive any of four actions, producing $4^5=1024$ functions. A stationary memoryless policy sees only the current symbol, not its occurrence count, and must select the same action each time. It has four possibilities. A controller with a clock can implement a nonstationary sequence, but that clock is internal state and is not part of a stationary current-percept-only rule.

title: Reachable histories versus all tables
stem: Two percepts are syntactically possible, but a deterministic environment always emits X on both of two decisions regardless of action. With three actions, count full tables on nonempty histories through length two and distinct behaviours in this environment.
solution: The full domain contains $2+4=6$ histories and therefore $3^6=729$ tables. Only X and XX are reachable. Behaviour in this environment is specified by the action on X and the action on XX, giving $3^2=9$ behaviours. Each behaviour is implemented by $3^4=81$ tables differing only at unreachable histories. The counts satisfy $9\cdot81=729$. Reachability is independent of action here by explicit assumption; in a general environment one must compute reachability under each policy before using this simplification.

title: Contingent policy count
stem: A two-stage decision has two first actions, three possible observations after either first action, and four second actions after each observation. Count full deterministic contingent policies and fixed action sequences.
solution: Choose the first action in two ways. For that chosen action, select one of four second actions separately for each of three possible observations, giving $4^3$ continuations. There are $2\cdot4^3=128$ contingent policies. A fixed sequence ignores the observation, so it has only $2\cdot4=8$ possibilities. This counts executable policies from the given start, not a table assigning unused continuations after the first action that was not chosen. Such a larger table would contain behaviourally irrelevant entries and would have a different count.

title: Counting a specified finite controller
stem: A deterministic Moore controller has two labelled internal states, three percepts and two actions. It updates state from the old internal state and current percept, then outputs the action assigned to the new state. Count syntactic controllers, including the initial internal state.
solution: The update table has $2\cdot3=6$ entries, each selecting one of two internal states, giving $2^6$ possibilities. The action table has two entries, each selecting one of two actions, giving $2^2$ possibilities. The initial internal state has two choices. Multiply to obtain $2\cdot2^6\cdot2^2=512$. This is a labelled syntactic count: isomorphic state renamings or unreachable internal states can implement the same behaviour. A Mealy controller whose output also depends directly on the percept has another signature and must be counted separately.

title: Vacuum configurations and belief subsets
stem: A two-room vacuum has a labelled position and two independent dirt bits. Count physical states, nonempty belief subsets, and the physical states compatible with percept (L, clean).
solution: The physical count is $2\cdot2\cdot2=8$. Every subset of these eight states is a syntactically possible set belief, so there are $2^8-1=255$ nonempty subsets. The given percept fixes position L and dirt bit $d_L=0$, leaving $d_R$ free. Exactly two states remain: $(L,0,0)$ and $(L,0,1)$. Neither $255$ nor two is the physical state-space size. Moreover, not all $255$ subsets must be reachable under the particular transition and sensor model.

title: Exactly k dirty rooms
stem: A robot can occupy any of six labelled rooms, and exactly two rooms are dirty. Count configurations when occupation of a dirty room is allowed, and when the robot must occupy a clean room.
solution: With unrestricted location, choose the two dirty rooms in $\binom62=15$ ways and then choose any of six locations, giving $90$. Under the clean-location condition, each dirty-room choice leaves four allowed locations, giving $15\cdot4=60$. Equivalently, choose the robot's location first in six ways and select two dirty rooms among the other five: $6\binom52=60$. The equality checks the constraint count. Multiplying $6\cdot2^6$ would include dirt patterns with the wrong number of dirty rooms.

title: Constraints can couple choices
stem: An elevator has ten possible stopped floors and one aggregate moving state. At a stopped floor its doors may be open or closed. While moving they must be closed. Count legal states and explain why this is not a complete route-planning state.
solution: There are $10\cdot2=20$ stopped states and one legal moving state, giving $21$. The naive product $11\cdot2=22$ includes the forbidden moving-with-open-doors combination. For route planning, one aggregate moving state generally omits the direction and the segment or destination, so its next floor is not determined. The count is correct for the explicitly declared coarse status model, but it does not establish that the model is sufficient for predicting elevator movement.

title: Labelled robots and collision exclusions
stem: Two labelled robots occupy distinct rooms among four, and each room has an independent dirt bit. Count states. When can the robots be treated as indistinguishable?
solution: Choose the first robot's room in four ways and the second's in three, then choose four dirt bits in $2^4$ ways. The count is $4\cdot3\cdot16=192$. If exchanging robot labels preserves actions, dynamics, sensor roles and performance, unordered occupied-room sets have $\binom42=6$ choices and the quotient count is $6\cdot16=96$. Different batteries, capacities or destinations can invalidate that symmetry. The smaller count is justified by a model invariance, not by the robots merely looking similar.

title: Expected utility despite an unlucky outcome
stem: Safe pays 4 certainly. Risky pays 10 with probability 3/5 and −2 otherwise. Under utility equal to the numerical payoff, which action is rational? Does a realized −2 refute that answer?
solution: Compute the risky expectation by weighting both outcomes: $(3/5)10+(2/5)(-2)=6-4/5=26/5$. Safe has expectation $4=20/5$, so risky is better by $6/5$. A realized loss of −2 has probability $2/5$ under the model and is compatible with the optimal decision. To challenge the decision, one would need to challenge the probabilities, utilities, available alternatives or evaluation criterion. Judging the choice using future information the agent did not have confuses rationality with omniscience.

title: A threshold different from one half
stem: Action A pays 12 in H and −4 in L. Action B pays 5 in either state. Let $P(H)=p$. Derive the entire optimal-action set, including boundaries.
solution: The expectations are $EU(A)=12p-4(1-p)=16p-4$ and $EU(B)=5$. Their difference is $16p-9$. Thus B is uniquely optimal for $0\le p<9/16$, both are optimal at $p=9/16$, and A is uniquely optimal for $9/16<p\le1$. At $p=0$, A pays −4 and B pays 5; at $p=1$, A pays 12 and B pays 5, checking the inequality direction. Merely testing whether $p$ exceeds one half would choose A incorrectly throughout $(1/2,9/16)$.

title: A negative coefficient reverses the inequality
stem: A pays $(1,9)$ in states H,L, while B pays $(4,4)$. Find when A is preferred, and explain the boundary case.
solution: Here $EU(A)=p+9(1-p)=9-8p$ and $EU(B)=4$. The comparison $9-8p\ge4$ becomes $-8p\ge-5$. Dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality, giving $p\le5/8$. Both actions tie at $5/8$; A is unique below it and B unique above it. The endpoint check $p=1$ gives A=1 and B=4, confirming that A cannot be the high-p action. The algebraic sign has a concrete interpretation: increasing H probability hurts A.

title: Weak dominance and zero-probability states
stem: A pays $(7,3)$ and B pays $(7,1)$ in H,L. Is A always strictly better in expectation? Identify all ties.
solution: A is at least as good in both states and strictly better in L. The expectation difference is $2P(L)=2(1-p)$. It is positive for $p<1$, but equals zero when $p=1$. Thus weak statewise dominance implies no lower expectation, not unconditional strict preference. At $p=1$, L has no probability and its payoff difference contributes nothing. If a later observation assigns L positive posterior mass, the strict comparison can reappear.

title: Positive affine utility transformation
stem: Prove that replacing outcome utility $U$ by $3U-7$ preserves expected-utility action rankings. Why does this proof not cover squaring arbitrary utility values?
solution: For each action, expectation is linear, so $E[3U-7]=3E[U]-7$. Subtract the transformed expectations of A and B: the constants cancel and the difference is $3(E[U_A]-E[U_B])$. Multiplication by positive three preserves its sign and every tie. Squaring is nonlinear, so $E[U^2]$ is not generally $(E[U])^2$; it also fails to be increasing over all real utilities. For instance utilities −2 and −1 reverse order after squaring. Even an increasing nonlinear transformation on a restricted domain can change lottery rankings.

title: Increasing outcome transformations can reverse lotteries
stem: Lottery A pays 0 or 100 equally likely; B pays 40 certainly. Compare expected money and expected square-root utility.
solution: Expected money is $50$ for A and $40$ for B, so a money-linear decision maker chooses A. With $u(x)=\sqrt{x}$, A has expected utility $(0+10)/2=5$, while B has $\sqrt{40}$. Since $40>25$, $\sqrt{40}>5$, so B is preferred. The square-root function is increasing on nonnegative outcomes, preserving their certain-outcome order, but it is not affine and changes risk tradeoffs. Neither preference is inconsistent with rationality once the corresponding utility is specified.

title: Expected utility versus maximin
stem: A pays $(8,-2)$, B pays $(3,3)$, and $P(H)=4/5$. Compare the expected-utility and maximin choices.
solution: The expectation of A is $(4/5)8+(1/5)(-2)=6$, whereas B has expectation 3. Expected utility selects A. The worst payoff of A is −2 and of B is 3, so maximin selects B. Maximin does not use the supplied prior; it protects against the worst state. The conflict is a difference in criterion, not a calculation error. Without probabilities or an alternative criterion, a payoff table alone does not select a unique rational action.

title: Minimax regret is not maximin
stem: Payoffs in H,L are A=$(10,0)$, B=$(6,5)$, C=$(0,8)$. Compute maximum regret and identify the minimax-regret action.
solution: The best payoff in H is 10 and in L is 8. Subtract each payoff from the best in the same state. A has regrets $(0,8)$, B has $(4,3)$ and C has $(10,0)$. Their maximum regrets are 8,4,10, so B uniquely minimizes worst regret. The worst payoffs are 0,5,0, so maximin happens to choose B here too, but for a different calculation. Regret must use statewise best payoffs; subtracting one global maximum 10 from both columns would create the wrong L regrets.

title: An objective proxy rewards the wrong action
stem: An agent can Clean, Announce or Stop. Clean removes one unit of dirt and costs 2; Announce changes no dirt and costs 0. A proposed reward is 3 per announcement. Over three actions, compare the reward-maximizing behaviour with maximizing dirt removed minus cost.
solution: Under the proposed proxy, three announcements yield 9 and dominate any sequence using Clean or Stop, which do not earn announcement reward. The world may remain dirty throughout. Under the alternative score “dirt removed minus cost”, one Clean gives $1-2=-1$, so with these numbers Stop gives the best score zero. This second criterion is also not a specification that prioritizes cleaning: its reward is too small to justify the cost. If cleaning is required, impose it as a goal/constraint or assign a consistent benefit. The analysis must inspect the actual numeric objective rather than assume its name expresses the desired behaviour.

title: A finite penalty is not a hard constraint
stem: A safe delivery yields 20. An unsafe delivery yields $30-M$. Find the penalty needed to prefer the safe action here, then explain why no fixed finite penalty handles arbitrarily large unsafe benefits.
solution: Safe is at least as good if $20\ge30-M$, so $M\ge10$; it is uniquely better if $M>10$. At $M=10$ the actions tie, so a policy may still choose unsafe unless the tie rule excludes it. If the unsafe benefit can be any $B$, its penalized value is $B-M$. For any finite M, choose $B>20+M$ and unsafe wins. A hard safety constraint removes unsafe choices irrespective of reward magnitude. Finite penalties can enforce safety only with a justified bound and suitable tie handling.

title: Known is independent of deterministic
stem: Classify a fair die with a known distribution and a door with an unknown but fixed code along the known/unknown and deterministic/stochastic axes. State the modelling assumptions.
solution: The die model assigns probability $1/6$ to each result under a roll. Its distribution is known, but the transition is stochastic. The door opens exactly when the entered code matches its fixed code. If the code is part of the physical state and the actuator is reliable, the transition is deterministic; the agent initially lacks the parameter. It is therefore unknown to that agent. A belief distribution over possible codes represents epistemic uncertainty and does not by itself make the fully specified door physics stochastic. Adding mechanical failure would change the transition model.

title: Hidden determinism can produce predictive uncertainty
stem: A hidden bit Z is sampled once with $P(Z=1)=3/4$ and then remains fixed. The action Reveal deterministically emits Z. Is uncertainty about the next observation proof of a stochastic transition after Z is included in state?
solution: No. Conditional on the full state $Z=0$ or $Z=1$, Reveal has a unique observation and leaves the bit unchanged. The agent's predictive distribution is $P(o=1)=3/4$ because it does not know which fixed state is actual. Initial-state uncertainty produces a mixture of deterministic possibilities. If Reveal is repeated after the first result, the next result is certain under the model; treating each result as an independent Bernoulli draw would incorrectly allow the bit to change. The initial sampling can be stochastic while subsequent state transitions are deterministic.

title: A static puzzle changes after action
stem: A sliding puzzle changes only when the agent moves a tile. It remains unchanged while the agent computes. Is it static? What changes if a score decreases once per second of thought?
solution: The original task is static because no exogenous evolution occurs during deliberation. Its response to the agent's move is entirely compatible with static classification. If only the score decreases while the board remains fixed, the task is semidynamic: physical configuration is unchanged but performance depends on elapsed time. If elapsed time also makes moves illegal, represent time or deadlines in the state and describe that broader dynamics. The phrase “the environment ever changes” is too coarse to distinguish these cases.

title: Independent inputs with coupled decisions
stem: A classifier receives independent images, but can request at most two expensive annotations in a session of ten images. Is annotation choice episodic?
solution: No. Requesting an annotation uses part of the shared budget and changes the available actions on future images. The input distribution can remain independent while the decision problem is sequential. A sufficient state includes the remaining annotation budget and, for a finite horizon, the number of images remaining when future opportunities depend on it. Without the shared budget and with additive independent per-image losses, separate classification decisions could be episodic. Independence of observations is not independence of action consequences.

title: Discrete does not mean finite
stem: A sensor reports a nonnegative integer counter, and actions are Increment or Stop. Time advances in discrete steps. Is this a finite-state task? How does a cap at 20 change the answer?
solution: The uncapped state set $\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ is countably infinite and discrete. Two actions and discrete time do not make the state set finite. With a hard cap at 20 and Increment defined to leave 20 unchanged, the counter has exactly 21 states. A stop/termination flag would add states if retained separately; it should not be silently included or excluded. In a finite horizon H from zero, only counters up to H may be reachable even in the uncapped physical model.

title: Single controller, several bodies
stem: One central program chooses joint actions for three robots. An opposing team has its own program. Is the central program's task necessarily single-agent because it controls all three robots?
solution: It can treat its own three robots as one decision maker whose action is a triple. The independently controlled opposing team still creates a multi-agent interaction. The number of physical robots does not determine the number of strategic decision makers. If each robot has four possible commands and every joint combination is legal, the central action set has $4^3=64$ elements. Collision or communication constraints can remove combinations. A deterministic transition given both teams' joint commands does not remove uncertainty about the opponent's choice.

title: Partial observability without a memory advantage
stem: Two hidden states produce the same percept. In both states action A gives utility 5 and action B gives utility 1. Prove that a memoryless policy is rational for any belief over the two states.
solution: Let the first state's probability be p. Then $EU(A)=5p+5(1-p)=5$ and $EU(B)=p+(1-p)=1$. A is uniquely optimal for all $p\in[0,1]$. The sensor is partially informative because it cannot distinguish the states, yet that distinction is irrelevant to the optimal choice. Memory might estimate p more accurately, but no p changes the maximizing action. This counterexample refutes the universal claim that every partially observable task requires memory for rational action.

title: Aliased histories with incompatible optima
stem: The same current percept occurs after histories $h_1,h_2$. At $h_1$, utilities of A,B are $(10,0)$; at $h_2$, they are $(0,10)$. Can any current-percept-only deterministic or randomized rule be optimal at both histories?
solution: A deterministic rule outputs one action for that percept. A is uniquely optimal at the first history and B at the second, so neither fixed choice works at both. Let a randomized rule choose A with probability q. Its utility is $10q$ at $h_1$ and $10(1-q)$ at $h_2$. To reach the optimum ten at the first requires $q=1$, while at the second requires $q=0$. These conditions are incompatible. At least two distinguishable internal conditions, or an additional observation, are necessary to implement both optimal choices.

title: Overlapping optimal-action sets
stem: Three histories share one percept. Their maximizing sets are $\{A,B\}$, $\{B,C\}$ and $\{B,D\}$. Does a rational deterministic reflex rule exist? What if the third set becomes $\{A,D\}$?
solution: Intersect the three sets. In the first case, the only common action is B, so selecting B is optimal at every history despite their different states. After changing the third set, the intersection of the first two remains $\{B\}$, but B is absent from $\{A,D\}$; the full intersection is empty. Pairwise considerations are not a substitute for the common intersection over all relevant histories. The result presupposes that these maximizing sets correctly incorporate the same task objective and continuation horizon.

title: Goal achievement versus maintenance
stem: A trajectory visits Safe, Collision, Destination. Does it satisfy “eventually reach Destination” and “never enter Collision”? Can a terminal test using only the final location distinguish it from Safe, Destination?
solution: The first trajectory reaches Destination and satisfies the achievement goal. It violates the maintenance requirement because it visited Collision. Both trajectories have the same final location, so a terminal predicate depending only on that location cannot distinguish their safety histories. Retain an “ever collided” bit or evaluate the entire trajectory. If collisions are absorbing and prevent reaching Destination, the task changes; that additional transition assumption must be stated rather than inferred from the word collision.

title: A compiled reflex policy can implement planning
stem: A finite fully observed task has an optimal stationary policy computed offline. At runtime a table maps each observed state directly to its stored optimal action. Is runtime lookahead necessary for rationality?
solution: No. If the model, objective and sufficient state remain as assumed, the table implements the computed optimal policy directly. Its runtime mechanism is a state-conditioned response, although planning was used to construct it. Rationality concerns the chosen action under the task criterion, not whether the program visibly simulates futures every time. If the objective is finite-horizon and the optimal policy depends on time remaining, include time in the table key. An outdated model or incomplete percept can invalidate the offline policy's guarantee.

title: Model-based does not mean online planning
stem: A vacuum remembers whether each room has been verified clean, updates those bits from observations and applies fixed rules to move, clean or stop. Explain why it can be model-based and reflex at the same time.
solution: It is model-based because its persistent summary uses assumptions about cleaning, movement and whether dirt can recur. It is reflex in the architectural sense that action selection applies a rule to the updated internal condition rather than searching future action sequences at runtime. Memory and lookahead are separate design dimensions. If cleaning is unreliable, setting a clean bit from the command alone is unjustified; the controller must verify the result or represent uncertainty. Thus the model label requires actual transition/observation assumptions, not merely storing a variable.

title: Learning without physical stochasticity
stem: A robot explores a fixed deterministic maze whose map is initially unknown. Another robot navigates a stochastic maze with all transition probabilities supplied. Which one must learn a transition model?
solution: The first may need to acquire unknown map information to navigate effectively, although a particular easy goal could be achievable without learning the whole map. Determinism does not supply the missing map. The second already has its transition model; stochasticity alone does not require estimating it from experience. It can plan using the supplied probabilities. Both might learn useful policies or computational shortcuts, but those are separate tasks. “Must learn” needs a performance requirement and remaining opportunities, not only an environment label.

title: Exploration can cost more than it is worth
stem: An experiment costs 5 utility units. Even with perfect information, all remaining action choices could improve expected utility by at most 2. Is the experiment rational if it has no other benefit?
solution: The information-induced improvement is bounded above by 2, and the cost is 5. Thus the net gain is at most $2-5=-3$. Not experimenting weakly improves utility by at least three relative to this experiment under the assumptions. Unknown parameters do not create an unconditional obligation to explore. If the experiment also produces direct reward or changes future available actions, include those effects and recompute the bound; the conclusion relies on their explicit exclusion.

title: Computation has an opportunity cost
stem: A fast program selects an action worth 8 in expectation. A slower program selects an action worth 10, but delay costs 3. Compare net performance and give the general condition for using the slower computation.
solution: The fast program's net utility is 8. The slow program's net utility is $10-3=7$, so the fast program is better by one. In general let the expected improvement from extra computation be $\Delta$ and its total utility cost be c. Extra computation is worthwhile only if $\Delta>c$, with a tie at equality. This comparison must include environmental change during thought, computation cost and any deadline effects. Comparing only the selected action quality would omit part of the task performance.

title: Current position omits a key
stem: At room X, action Open reaches the goal only if a key was collected earlier. Two histories end at X, one with a key and one without. Show why position alone is not a sufficient state and give a sufficient augmentation for this rule.
solution: Both histories map to the same position X, yet the action's legality or successor differs depending on the key. Therefore no single transition $T(X,\text{Open})$ captures both histories exactly. Use state $(x,k)$ with a key bit $k\in\{0,1\}$, assuming all other future-relevant information is already encoded in x. The two histories become $(X,1)$ and $(X,0)$ and their different action outcomes are well-defined. This is a concrete violation of the Markov/sufficiency requirement, not merely a claim that history is generally useful.

title: Time can matter in stationary physics
stem: A project action pays −1 now and 5 at the following decision. A safe action pays 2 now and terminates. With undiscounted finite-horizon reward, compare the choices when one versus two decisions remain.
solution: With one decision remaining, the project's later reward lies outside the horizon, so its return is −1 and safe gives 2; safe wins. With two decisions remaining and the promised later reward guaranteed, project returns $-1+5=4$, exceeding safe's 2. The physical transition rule did not change, but the optimal action depends on remaining horizon. A stationary position-only policy cannot implement both choices at the same physical state. Use a time-indexed policy or augment state with the remaining decision count.

title: Distinct beliefs with identical support
stem: Hidden states are H,L and utilities are A=$(12,-4)$, B=$(5,5)$. Compare beliefs $P(H)=1/4$ and $P(H)=3/4$. Can a support set alone encode the optimal choice?
solution: Both beliefs have support $\{H,L\}$ because each state has positive probability. At $p=1/4$, $EU(A)=0$ and B=5, so choose B. At $p=3/4$, $EU(A)=8$ and B=5, so choose A. The common support set records possibility but not relative weight. A worst-case or guaranteed-goal task might use set beliefs appropriately, but an expected-utility task generally requires probabilities or another sufficient statistic retaining the decision-relevant weights.

title: Bayesian conditioning must include the prior
stem: Let $P(H)=3/10$, $P(+\mid H)=4/5$ and $P(+\mid L)=1/5$. Compute the positive-signal probability and the posterior of H. Explain why 4/5 is not the posterior.
solution: The joint positive masses are $(3/10)(4/5)=12/50$ in H and $(7/10)(1/5)=7/50$ in L. Their sum is $19/50$. Normalize the H mass: $P(H\mid+)= (12/50)/(19/50)=12/19$. The likelihood $4/5$ conditions on H and asks how often the signal is positive; the posterior conditions on a positive signal and asks how often H is true. These are different conditional probabilities, with the prior determining how much L contributes to observed positives.

title: The negative observation matters too
stem: Under the binary sensor in Question 39, derive the negative-signal probability and posterior, then verify that posterior averaging recovers the prior.
solution: Negative likelihoods are $1/5$ in H and $4/5$ in L. The H negative mass is $3/50$, the L negative mass is $28/50$, so $P(-)=31/50$ and $P(H\mid-)=3/31$. Average the posteriors with their signal probabilities: $(19/50)(12/19)+(31/50)(3/31)=12/50+3/50=15/50=3/10$. This is total probability applied to H. Averaging $12/19$ and $3/31$ equally would be wrong because the signal outcomes are not equally likely.

title: An impossible observation has no Bayesian posterior
stem: Both states H,L give a positive signal with probability one. An agent observes a negative signal. May it return posterior $P(H\mid-)=1/2$ by convention?
solution: The probability of a negative signal is zero for every prior because both negative likelihoods are zero. Bayes' formula has numerator zero and denominator zero, so it does not determine a posterior. A fabricated one-half answer is not a consequence of the model. Report an observation inconsistent with the model and investigate sensor errors or missing states. A revised model can introduce a small failure probability and yield a valid posterior, but its result depends on the specified failure probabilities, not a universal fallback.

title: Prediction before observation
stem: Initially $P(H)=1/4$. An action switches H to L with probability 1/5 and switches L to H with probability 2/5. A positive sensor has likelihoods 3/4 in H and 1/4 in L. Compute the posterior after the action and a positive result.
solution: Predict the new H probability first: $(1/4)(4/5)+(3/4)(2/5)=1/5+3/10=1/2$. The new L probability is also one half. Positive joint masses are $3/8$ for H and $1/8$ for L, totaling one half. Hence the posterior is $(3/8)/(1/2)=3/4$. Conditioning the old prior directly would give $(3/16)/(3/16+3/16)=1/2$, which is wrong because it ignores the state-changing action. Prediction and correction represent different stages of the control loop.

title: Optimize after each signal, then average
stem: Use prior $P(H)=3/10$, positive likelihoods $(4/5,1/5)$, and utilities A=$(12,-4)$, B=$(5,5)$. Find optimal expected utility before and after a free signal.
solution: Before sensing, A gives $16(3/10)-4=4/5$ and B gives 5, so prior optimum is 5. The positive posterior is $12/19$, giving A=$116/19>5$; choose A. The negative posterior is $3/31$, giving A=$-76/31<5$; choose B. Weight the optimized branch values: $(19/50)(116/19)+(31/50)5=271/50$. The gain is $21/50$. Averaging utilities for a fixed action before maximizing would yield the original value 5 and discard the ability to adapt the action to the signal.

title: Information cost and the exact tie
stem: For the model in Question 43, determine the complete sensor-purchase decision as a function of nonnegative cost c.
solution: Acting without the signal gives 5. Buying the signal gives net value $271/50-c$. Purchase is better when $271/50-c>5$, equivalently $c<21/50$. At $c=21/50$ the two choices tie. For larger cost, do not purchase. For example $c=1/4$ leaves gain $21/50-1/4=17/100$, whereas $c=1/2$ leaves $-2/25$. These comparisons assume utility costs share the same scale as the payoff table, and the sensor does not delay or alter the hidden state.

title: Perfect information bounds the signal value
stem: For A=$(12,-4)$, B=$(5,5)$ and $P(H)=3/10$, compute expected utility with perfect information and its gain over no information.
solution: Perfect information selects A in H, where 12 exceeds 5, and B in L, where 5 exceeds −4. The value is $(3/10)12+(7/10)5=71/10$. Without information, B gives 5, so perfect-information value is $71/10-5=21/10$. A noisy signal in the same costless one-step task cannot be more valuable than perfect state knowledge: a perfectly informed agent could generate the noisy observation according to its conditional law and imitate the noisy-signal policy. The upper bound concerns the same action set, utility and timing.

title: Useful sensing can have zero decision value
stem: The prior of H is 1/2. A pays $(10,9)$ and B pays $(0,8)$. A perfect sensor reveals H or L. Compute its decision value despite reducing uncertainty to zero.
solution: A dominates B strictly in both states, so the prior optimum is $E[A]=(10+9)/2=19/2$. After perfect sensing, A remains best in either state, yielding the same weighted value $19/2$. The information value is zero. The signal eliminates state uncertainty but does not change the action or the achieved utility. Any positive sensing cost makes it undesirable under this criterion. Information-theoretic uncertainty reduction and decision value are distinct quantities.

title: Prove nonnegative free-information value
stem: Assume a finite one-step task, a costless signal with no physical effect or delay, and permission to ignore it. Prove its optimized expected value cannot be below the prior optimum.
solution: Let $a_0$ maximize prior expected utility. For each positive-probability signal y, conditional optimization gives $\max_a E[U(a)\mid y]\ge E[U(a_0)\mid y]$. Multiply by $P(y)$ and sum. The right side becomes $E[U(a_0)]$ by total expectation; the left side is optimized signal value. Their difference is nonnegative. The proof also shows why permission to ignore the signal matters: following $a_0$ remains feasible. A sensing cost, forced action change, delay or model mismatch needs its own analysis and is outside these hypotheses.

title: Randomization cannot beat a one-step maximum
stem: Two actions have expected utilities 7 and 3 in a fixed single-agent one-step model. Can randomizing strictly improve expected utility? State a limitation of the conclusion.
solution: Choosing the first action with probability q gives utility $7q+3(1-q)=3+4q$, which is at most 7 for $q\in[0,1]$ and equals 7 only at q=1. More generally, a convex combination of fixed expected utilities cannot exceed their maximum. This assumes the environment response and probabilities do not depend on the mixing strategy. In a strategic game, an opponent may exploit a predictable choice, and changing the mixture can change the effective payoff; the fixed single-agent argument then does not apply unchanged.

title: Sensorless vacuum plan by exact belief propagation
origin: Reconstructed Edinburgh INF2D Lecture 2 vacuum example; independently numbered states and proof
stem: In the deterministic two-room vacuum model, start with every physical state possible. Prove that Right, Clean, Left, Clean reaches the clean goal without observations.
solution: Initially there are eight possibilities. Right maps all of them to position R while preserving dirt, leaving four distinct states. Clean sets right dirt to zero, leaving two states differing only in left dirt. Left changes position to L, still leaving two states. The final Clean sets left dirt to zero, leaving the single state $(L,0,0)$. Every initial possibility reaches the goal. This proof uses reliable movement, reliable cleaning, idempotent boundary moves and no dirt reappearance. A failed actuator or spontaneous dirt would require a different belief update and invalidate the guarantee.

title: Shortest plan from a known dirty configuration
stem: From $(L,1,1)$, both rooms are dirty and actions Clean and movement cost one. Give a minimum-cost plan to clean both and prove optimality.
solution: Clean, Right, Clean reaches $(R,0,0)$ with cost three. Any solution must clean each initially dirty room at least once, requiring at least two Clean actions. Because one action cleans only the currently occupied room, the agent must also move between rooms at least once. Therefore every solution costs at least three, matching the exhibited plan. The proof would change if one action could clean both rooms or if a room became clean without action. An additional return-to-left requirement would raise the minimum to four.

title: A locally clean room does not justify stopping
stem: The percept is (L, clean). The unobserved right room is dirty with probability p. Moving right costs 1, cleaning if needed costs 1, and removing right-room dirt yields benefit 6. Assume a free perfect local observation on arrival. When is a visit worthwhile?
solution: Stopping gives utility zero relative to the current state. Visiting always pays movement cost one. With probability p, the room is dirty and cleaning yields net $6-1=5$; otherwise no cleaning occurs. Expected net value is $-1+5p$. A visit is strictly worthwhile for $p>1/5$, tied at $p=1/5$, and worse for smaller p. The policy is contingent because it cleans only after observing dirt. Charging cleaning cost in every branch would produce an incorrect threshold; forgetting movement cost would incorrectly favour every positive p.

title: Stopping requires a model assumption
stem: A controller has observed both rooms clean and stops forever. Under what condition is this sound for maintaining cleanliness? Give a failure case.
solution: If cleaning observations are reliable and dirt never reappears, the stored clean bits remain valid and stopping maintains the goal. If each clean room can become dirty spontaneously after a decision, prior observations do not guarantee future cleanliness. For example, right-room dirt can appear immediately after the last observation; Stop then leaves a dirty room. The controller must include a recurrence model, sensing or revisiting policy and a stated performance tradeoff. “Both rooms were clean” is a statement about a past or current state, not a universal future invariant without transition assumptions.

title: Belief-set update can merge states
stem: Initial possibilities are $(L,0,0)$ and $(R,0,0)$. Right reliably sets position R. What is the resulting belief set, and why does mapping a set not preserve its cardinality?
solution: Both initial states map to $(R,0,0)$, so the resulting belief is the singleton $\{(R,0,0)\}$. A deterministic transition is a function but need not be injective. Set images remove duplicate successors; two possibilities can merge. Conversely, a deterministic action cannot increase the cardinality of a finite belief set before observations, while a nondeterministic action can branch one state into several. These facts concern support sets, not a claim that entropy always decreases under every operation.

title: Observation filtering versus state prediction
stem: A belief contains $(L,1,0),(L,0,1),(R,1,1)$. The agent executes Right, then observes the right room clean. Find the posterior belief set in the reliable vacuum model.
solution: First propagate Right to obtain $(R,1,0),(R,0,1),(R,1,1)$. The right-clean percept retains only states with $d_R=0$, leaving $\{(R,1,0)\}$. Filtering the original states for current position R before predicting would retain only $(R,1,1)$ and then wrongly conclude the clean observation impossible. The new observation describes the state after the previous action, so prediction must precede filtering. The result tells us the left room remains dirty even though the sensor is local, because the prior possibilities and action constrain it.

title: An exact abstraction must preserve legality
stem: An abstraction merges key-present and key-absent states at one door. Open is legal only with the key. Explain why defining the abstract legal actions as their union can create a false solution.
solution: The union includes Open because it is legal in the key-present state. The abstract state then admits a plan beginning with Open. If the actual detailed state lacks the key, that first step cannot execute. The plan is therefore not uniformly realizable from all detailed states represented by the abstract state. An exact abstraction needs matching legal actions for equivalent states, or an explicit refinement/precondition that distinguishes the cases. A relaxed union can be useful for lower-bound reasoning, but must not be presented as an exact executable plan model.

title: Transition agreement without cost agreement is insufficient
stem: Two detailed states map to abstract X. Both permit action a and reach abstract goal G. The action costs 1 from one detailed state and 9 from the other. Can the abstraction assign one exact cost to edge X→G?
solution: No single number equals both detailed costs. Successor and goal agreement preserve reachability here, but not exact path cost. Assigning cost one is a lower bound for the second state, while assigning nine overestimates the first. Either retain the variable causing the difference, use a state-conditioned refinement, or explicitly label a relaxed cost model. The claim being preserved matters: an abstraction may correctly answer “can the goal be reached?” while giving incorrect optimal-cost answers.

title: Goal disagreement breaks abstraction
stem: Two states share the same location, but one has completed all deliveries and the other has not. A location-only goal test marks that location as a goal. Identify the error and a repair.
solution: The abstraction merges states with different goal status, so its goal predicate is not well-defined as an exact representation. It accepts the incomplete-delivery state. Retain a bit mask of unfinished deliveries, or another sufficient task-progress summary, and define the goal as the empty mask at the required location. If every delivery is uniquely determined by location under additional rules, the mask may be redundant, but that must be proved. A convenient goal test cannot recover information intentionally discarded by the state representation.

title: Depth and cost can rank plans differently
stem: Plan A has two actions costing 100 each. Plan B has three actions costing one each. Which is shallowest and which is cheapest? Under what simple condition do depth and cost always agree?
solution: A has depth two and cost 200. B has depth three and cost three. Thus A is shallower while B is cheaper. If every action has the same strictly positive cost c, a depth-d plan has cost cd, so minimizing depth and minimizing cost coincide. Zero common cost makes all costs tie regardless of depth; negative common cost favours longer paths and can fail to admit a minimum with cycles. The positive-cost condition is essential to strict agreement.

title: A finite graph can generate an infinite search tree
stem: A state graph has vertices X and G, with actions X→X and X→G. Count distinct states and the number of distinct finite solution paths. Explain the difference from search nodes.
solution: There are two physical states. For every nonnegative integer k, taking the self-loop k times and then moving to G gives a distinct finite action sequence. Thus there are infinitely many solution paths and corresponding search-tree prefixes even though the state graph is finite. If the self-loop costs one, the zero-loop solution is cheapest; if it costs zero, all these solutions have equal cost; if it costs −1, their costs decrease without bound and no minimum exists. Search nodes retain path identity rather than merely naming a state.

title: Zero-length solution versus failure
stem: A search API returns an empty action list both when the initial state is already a goal and when no goal is reachable. Explain the ambiguity and specify a repair.
solution: An empty list is a valid zero-cost plan when the initial state satisfies the goal, because no action is needed. For an unreachable goal it does not denote a successful plan. Returning the same untagged value prevents the caller from deciding whether to celebrate completion or report failure. Use an explicit failure sentinel distinct from lists, or a result object containing a success flag and action list. If failure uses null, an empty list can consistently mean a successful zero-length plan.

title: Finite-horizon policy count
stem: There are four states and three legal actions in every state. Count stationary deterministic state policies and fully specified nonstationary deterministic policies over two decision times.
solution: A stationary policy assigns an action independently to four states, giving $3^4=81$. A time-indexed policy assigns an action to each of four states at each of two times, giving $3^{4\cdot2}=6561$. This is a full-table count including unreachable state-time pairs. If an episode terminates in certain states, action entries there may be omitted under a different convention. Nonstationarity expands the representational possibilities; it does not prove the optimum actually needs every additional degree of freedom.

title: Legal action counts vary by state
stem: Three states have 2, 3 and 1 legal actions respectively. Count stationary deterministic policies. Why is $3^3$ incorrect?
solution: Each state has its own permitted choices, so multiply $2\cdot3\cdot1=6$. The maximum branching factor three is not the legal action count at all states. Raising it to the number of states gives an upper bound 27 containing illegal assignments. If a terminal state is represented by zero legal actions, define whether its policy entry is omitted or a special Stop action is included; an unqualified product containing zero would otherwise suggest no policy exists even for a normally terminating task.

title: Discount changes a sequential choice
stem: Action A gives rewards 6 now and −10 next; B gives 1 now and 8 next. For $0\le\gamma\le1$, find the preferred action under two-step discounted return.
solution: Returns are $G_A=6-10\gamma$ and $G_B=1+8\gamma$. Subtract to obtain $5-18\gamma$. A is unique for $\gamma<5/18$, both tie at $5/18$, and B is unique for larger gamma. At gamma zero only the immediate reward matters and A wins. At gamma one, A returns −4 while B returns 9. This demonstrates why a greedy immediate-reward comparison is insufficient once future consequences count.

title: Bounding an infinite discounted return
stem: Rewards satisfy $|r_t|\le3$ and discount is $\gamma=4/5$. Prove an absolute bound on the infinite return and on the omitted tail after the first ten rewards.
solution: The triangle inequality gives $|G|\le\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}3(4/5)^t=3/(1-4/5)=15$. After rewards at indices 0 through 9, the remaining absolute tail is at most $\sum_{t=10}^{\infty}3(4/5)^t=15(4/5)^{10}$. This bound is deterministic and therefore also bounds the absolute expected tail. It relies on bounded rewards and a discount below one. With gamma one, the same estimate diverges; a finite horizon or other convergence assumption is required.

title: Random terminal time complicates reward shifts
stem: Policy A receives reward 1 then terminates. Policy B receives rewards 0,0 then terminates. Compare undiscounted returns before and after adding 2 to every executed step reward. Does this contradict affine utility invariance?
solution: Original returns are 1 for A and 0 for B, so A wins. After the per-step shift, A returns 3 while B returns 4, so B wins. The total added quantity is two times the episode length, which differs by policy. Therefore the transformation is not one common affine transformation of complete-run utility. If both runs had the same fixed length, a common per-step shift would add the same constant and preserve ranking. Affine invariance applies to outcome/run utilities under one common transformation, not arbitrary policy-dependent additions.

title: Probability of success versus expected reward
stem: A succeeds with probability 9/10 and pays 1 on success, 0 otherwise. B succeeds with probability 1/2 and pays 4 on success, 0 otherwise. Compare maximizing success probability and maximizing the stated expected payoff.
solution: Success probability favours A because $9/10>1/2$. Expected payoff gives A=$9/10$ and B=$2$, favouring B. If utility were the success indicator for both actions, expected utility would equal success probability and select A. Here the stated rewards differ in magnitude, so the two objectives are not identical. “Goal achievement” must specify whether only success counts or whether different successful outcomes have different value.

title: Information cannot repair impossible actuation
stem: A sensor reveals the hidden state perfectly, but the agent has only one legal action. Can the signal improve optimized one-step decision utility if it has no direct environmental effect?
solution: With one legal action a, both before and after the signal the agent must choose a. Averaging conditional utility gives $\sum_yP(y)E[U(a)\mid y]=E[U(a)]$, so decision value is zero. The signal can improve predictions or explanations but cannot change the outcome through action in this model. A new actuator, a timing choice or a future action opportunity would change the feasible policy set and could make information valuable. Sensors and actuators affect different sides of the decision problem.

title: Observation accuracy is not task value
stem: The prior of H is 1/100. A pays 1 in H and −100 in L; B pays 0 in both. A sensor is correct with probability 9/10 in either state. Is a positive sensor result enough to choose A?
solution: Positive H mass is $9/1000$ and positive L mass is $99/1000$, so the posterior is $9/108=1/12$. A is preferred only when $p-100(1-p)\ge0$, or $p\ge100/101$. The posterior $1/12$ is far below that threshold, so choose B after the positive signal. A nominally 90%-accurate sensor is not the same as a 90% posterior, and even a high posterior might be insufficient under a large false-positive loss. Prior rarity and utility asymmetry both matter.

title: Optimal action under an interval of priors
stem: A pays $(12,-4)$ and B pays $(5,5)$. The prior p is only known to lie in $[1/4,3/4]$. Choose a fixed action by maximin expected utility over that interval.
solution: A has expectation $16p-4$, increasing in p, so its worst expectation on the interval occurs at $p=1/4$ and equals zero. B has expectation five throughout. Maximin over the stated prior uncertainty chooses B. At the single known prior $p=3/4$, expected utility would instead choose A with value eight. Robust optimization over a set of plausible priors is a different problem from substituting the interval midpoint or optimizing separately at each prior without knowing which applies.

title: Sensitivity of expected utility to probability error
stem: For A=$(12,-4)$ and B=$(5,5)$, a model estimates $\widehat p$ with $|p-\widehat p|\le\varepsilon$. Bound the error in the A-versus-B expected-utility difference. When is the estimated preference certified?
solution: The difference is $D(p)=16p-9$. Thus $|D(p)-D(\widehat p)|=16|p-\widehat p|\le16\varepsilon$. If $D(\widehat p)>16\varepsilon$, the true difference stays positive, certifying A. If $D(\widehat p)<-16\varepsilon$, it stays negative, certifying B. Otherwise the uncertainty interval may cross the tie threshold and the sign is not certified by this bound. For $\widehat p=3/5$ and $\varepsilon=1/100$, estimated difference is $3/5$, exceeding $4/25$, so A is certified.

title: A maintenance property needs trajectory information
stem: A navigation model has ten positions. To distinguish whether any collision has occurred, add a Boolean flag. Count the syntactic augmented states, and explain why the count may exceed the reachable count.
solution: The Cartesian product has $10\cdot2=20$ position-flag combinations. The transition updates the flag by logical OR with whether the new step collides; once true, it remains true. A start with flag false may not reach every flagged position if the map prevents collisions or if collision terminates the episode. Therefore 20 is the syntactic representation count, not necessarily the reachable count. The augmentation makes the property “no collision has ever occurred” a current-state predicate, enabling a terminal test to evaluate the history requirement.

title: Joint actions with a shared resource
stem: Three labelled robots independently choose Idle or Charge, but at most one may charge at a time. Count legal joint actions and compare with the unconstrained product.
solution: The unconstrained product has $2^3=8$ triples. Legal choices are all Idle, or exactly one specified robot charging. There is one all-idle choice and three one-charge choices, for four legal actions. Equivalently sum $\binom30+\binom31=4$. Multiplying per-robot action counts ignores the shared charger constraint. If at most two robots could charge, the count would become $1+3+3=7$, excluding only all three charging.

title: Current observation versus remembered parameter
stem: A robot sees its exact position but does not know whether the movement command is reversed. Is the task fully observable, known, both or neither? Explain how the answer depends on the declared state.
solution: If the state is declared to be position and the reversal is an unknown fixed transition parameter, position is fully observed but the dynamics are unknown. If the physical state includes the hidden reversal bit, the same sensor does not reveal the full augmented state, so the task is partially observable as well. Both descriptions can model the same situation at different levels. State the representation before assigning labels. Learning the reversal may make the agent's effective model known without changing the physical sensor.

title: Changing the objective changes sufficient state
stem: A robot's map and position suffice to reach a fixed destination. The objective changes to collecting every token before arrival. What extra state is generally required, and why is token count alone insufficient?
solution: Retain the set or bit mask of remaining token locations. Two histories can have the same position and the same number of remaining tokens but leave tokens in different rooms. Their optimal next routes and goal status after a move can differ. A count alone loses the identity needed for transitions and planning. If the token locations are symmetric under all relevant dynamics and goals, a smaller quotient may be justified, but not in a general map. Sufficient state is relative to the objective as well as the physical movement model.

title: A constrained elevator with a sufficient moving state
origin: Reconstruction of CMU 15-281 Lecture 1 activity, with new data and explicit transition requirements
stem: An elevator has six floors, two door states when stopped, and five between-floor segments with two movement directions each. Moving doors must be closed. Count configurations, then state what further information a passenger-serving task may need.
solution: Stopped configurations number $6\cdot2=12$. Moving configurations number $5\cdot2=10$, since each segment permits up or down and only a closed-door state. Total is 22. A continuous physical model may also need position within the segment and velocity; the stated discrete segment model intentionally abstracts those. Passenger service additionally needs outstanding requests, occupancy, capacity and possibly destination commitments. The count is exact for the specified configuration variables, not proof that those variables suffice for every elevator objective.

title: A simple rule can encode a winning plan
origin: Reconstruction of CMU 15-281 candy activity, changed initial count and independently proved pattern
stem: Two players alternately remove one or two counters; taking the last wins. With 14 counters and perfect play, give a winning first action and prove the pattern without enumerating the whole game tree.
solution: Zero counters is losing for the player to move. By induction, positive multiples of three are losing: either legal removal leaves a nonmultiple, while any nonmultiple can remove its remainder modulo three to leave a multiple. After the opponent removes one or two, respond with two or one so each pair removes three. Since 14 has remainder two, remove two and leave 12. This proves a winning rule for this finite normal-play game. It illustrates how an offline proof can yield a tiny reactive policy; reversing the last-counter rule changes the base case and the strategy.

title: A board arrangement need not be a full chess state
origin: Reconstruction of Edinburgh INF2D Lecture 1 chess discussion, with explicit state-sufficiency analysis
stem: Two chess histories produce the same piece arrangement and side to move, but in one history a king moved and returned, and in the other it never moved. Can arrangement and side to move determine every legal move?
solution: No. Castling eligibility depends on whether the king or relevant rook moved previously, even if the pieces returned to the same squares. When all other castling conditions hold, one history permits castling and the other does not. Therefore the proposed state merges different legal-action sets. Include castling rights, en-passant information and relevant draw-history information according to the rules being modelled. This does not make standard chess intrinsically hidden-information; a full publicly known rule state can include those history summaries.

title: A transition distribution must be normalized
origin: Reconstruction of Stanford CS221 Markov Decisions modelling, independently constructed data
stem: A proposed stochastic action has successor weights 2,3,5. Turn them into a transition distribution and calculate expected successor utility for utilities 4,0,−2. What if the entries were already claimed to be probabilities?
solution: As nonnegative weights, divide by the total ten to get probabilities $1/5,3/10,1/2$. The expected utility is $(1/5)4+(3/10)0+(1/2)(-2)=4/5-1=-1/5$. If 2,3,5 were literally asserted to be probabilities, the model is invalid: values exceed one and sum to ten. Normalization is justified for declared weights, not an automatic repair of any flawed probability statement. The transition distribution also needs an explicit successor-state association for each entry.

title: Bounded implementability changes the optimization domain
origin: Reconstruction of Michael Wooldridge Lecture 2 bounded-agent distinction, independently constructed data
stem: Three behavioural functions have expected utilities 9,8,6. Only the latter two can be implemented within a specified architecture's memory and deadline. Identify the unrestricted and bounded optima. What changes if the utility-9 function becomes implementable?
solution: Over all three functions, the unrestricted optimum is the utility-9 function. Over the implementable subset, the best is the utility-8 function. This is a restriction of the feasible optimization domain, not an assertion that eight is globally best. If the utility-9 function becomes implementable without changing utilities or costs, the bounded optimum rises to nine. Enlarging a feasible set cannot lower its maximum when the objective is unchanged. If additional hardware costs utility, include them before making that monotonicity comparison.

title: Synthesis: choose representation, sensor and action
origin: Original hard mathematical and conceptual synthesis
stem: A hidden condition H has prior 3/10. Action A gives $(12,-4)$ and B gives $(5,5)$. A sensor has positive likelihoods $(4/5,1/5)$ and costs 1/4. The condition stays fixed while sensing. Specify a complete optimal policy, its expected net utility, the information state required and one assumption whose removal invalidates the calculation.
solution: Without sensing, B is optimal at utility five. Positive-signal probability is $19/50$ and posterior $12/19$, which exceeds the decision threshold $9/16$, so take A. Negative probability is $31/50$ and posterior $3/31$, which is below the threshold, so take B. Optimized value after sensing is $271/50$, and net value is $271/50-1/4=517/100$, exceeding five by $17/100$. Thus buy the sensor, then execute the contingent action rule. A sufficient information state includes the posterior or, for this fixed single-use model, the observed signal and known prior/likelihoods. A generic current percept unrelated to the signal is insufficient. If H can change during sensing, first predict its new distribution; if sensor delay costs utility, subtract that too. The conclusion is exact for the stated finite model.
